Monday
January 9, 1950
Today we got off to an 8:00 a.m. start by cer - a
Chrysler - to a most wonderful experience.
We drove along the road
which leads to Beirut in Lebanon and about half way turned north behind
the coastal range and on to Balbek, an old Roman ruin which should be -
we all think - as well known as any historic place. It was built on
the most tremendous plan and took over two hundred years and as many
thousands of sleves to complete.
It is in a truly remarkable state of
preservetion. The first structure was built around 200 B.C. and the
whole temple wes finally completed around 500 A.D. Some idea of its
size can be goined by the fact that the stairs leading to the temple
were 150' wide and the great courtyard approximately 100 yards in
each direction. One of the buildings - the temple of Bacchus - des-
cribed as "perhaps the most beautiful of all the temples surviving
from Roman times" is in a good state of preservation.
Even a small
part of the roof is still in place.
The whole place is fascinating,
but it would take a small book to describe it properly. However, one
item will give you some idea of the prodigious effort expended.
Many of the columns were fashioned from limestone in a quarry within
sight of the temple.

The
pillars - which, by the way, were decorated after they were put in
place - were carried on barges down the Nile, landed at Tyre in
southern Lebanon and rolled to Baalbek more than one hundred miles
along a road built for that purpose.
So much for Baalbek. You will hear more about it from
have a look at the latter city and its modern airport now under con-
struction we drove over there.
The airport is a long way from
complete but will be the best in this part of the world. The city
is often called "Little Paris". It is built along the blue Medi-
terranean shore with mountains rising three or four thousand feet
in the background.
There are several attractive seaside resort
hotels at one of which - the St. George - we had tea and picked up
a few shells on the beach. (For you collectors - no good ones !)
Driving back to Damascus "e got into a dense fog up in
the mountsins, but fortunately our Arab driver was good and we got
home about 8:00 p.m. all agreeing thst we have seen a lot considering
that we left Brussels only Saturday night and this is Monday!
will try to get off another femily letter from Delhi.
As ever,
н. м. В.
P.S.
We thought that Damascus - surrounded by desert - would be
warm but it was plenty cold and we nearly froze at Baalbek. Hebe
wore three sweaters, one of my coats, all her own coats and a rain-
coat on top of it all and still was cold!

Sunday
January 8, 1950
Dear Family,
We left Paris by Wegon Lits Friday night, arriving Brussels
early Saturday morning. Took off in a Constellation with thirty-five
of its forty-one seats filled at 5:00 pm, flew down
• the Rhone Valley
to Marseilles, across Corsica to Rome - Naples - Athens, across Cyprus,
over Beirut and after a nine hour flight arrived at Damascus at 2:00
a.m. this morning.
One of the drawbacks to my travel in the past has been the
fact that I never quite enjoy any experience because I always wish so
much that the family were along to enjoy it too. Well, this time they
are - or at least the one most important member and ath of the others -
or I should say 1/7th because the two Bills and Sam are included.
We thought Damascus would not be crowded but it was. In
fact, we had to sit up until 5:00 a.m. to crawl into beds newly made up
after a plane departure at that hour.
We slept until about 10:00 a.m.,
had breakfest in our room not rooms
- because Hebe was quartered with
us, and then went out on the town with an English-speaking guide - one
Abraham Baho, a Syrian Christian. (When Hebe had trouble pronouncing
his last name he said, "Just call me 'Abrahem'.") Debby and Hebe were
enthusiastic over the native city - the Bazzar with its wonderful
shops and the second largest mosque in the world - the old church of
John the Baptist.
•We saw the over-sized tomb which they claim holds
the head of John
the Beptist, and we also saw the tomb of Saladin.
Then we went all through the
ex-sultan's palace and saw the quarters
where his thirty-five wives lived. Our guide told us several times
that the wives were never permitted to leave the paloce, but to me
that repetition was unnecessery. If those thirty-five wives had got
loose in those shops in the Bazzar the sultan would probably have become
a priest after the
bankruptcy proceedings! After a drive dow the
Street called Streight we had lunch - very good - then drove about
twenty-five miles out along the excellent highway which runs to
Bagdad,
turned off to e little mountain town called Malulah where
there is a small community the members of which - some five hundred
strong - still speak the language of Christ.
they have lived at the end of a fertile velley with their village at
the sheltered end and their Roman Catholic monastery high above on
We reached the church by walking up & narrow gorge
cut in the massive rocks by a mountain stream which was still there.
Along the trail there were numerous eaves, hollowed out of the solid
rock back in the days when the Romans were there. At the top, the
Shangri-la like monastery wes surrounded by hills many oi which were
snowspped. The view was magnificent.
The old Bishop - as fine a
looking character as you ever saw - had us served with twenty year old
wine and gave us some unleavened bread and cheese - all very good
indeed, especially the wine.
The latter is made on the place from
their own vineyards.
